findings.summary: Queued requests that used 'after <id>' to ask for real ordering silently lose that ordering
findings.evidence: Under the new rule, 'after <job>' is only a reference. The reading accepts this, and CHANGELOG.md says a request that needs ordering must write 'Depends on <job>'. Existing queued items that relied on 'after' get no warning. Showing the cited ids as references in `athena plan` would make the loss visible. This follows from the requested rule and is not a defect.

summary: The change does what was asked: a request that only cites a rejected or failed job no longer holds the item. This redoes the earlier job from base and fixes the cause in `plan_entry`. That function used to treat every full job id in the request text as a dependency. It now counts only two things, through a new function `dependency_ids_in`: ids on a line that starts with "Depends on", and the job named in a "try again on <id>" request. Lines are matched in any case, after an optional `>`, list marker, bold marks or number. How held items are refused, the reason text and the retry rule are unchanged. New tests cover each case: a cited id is planned, a "Depends on" line naming a rejected job is still held with the right reason until a retry lands, and the retry link stays a dependency. Each of them fails on base. Old tests that used "after <id>" now use "Depends on". The `plan_entry` doc comment, the `plan.rs` module doc and CHANGELOG.md all state the new rule. I ran the new and updated core and drain tests and they pass; Athena's recorded fmt, clippy and full test runs also passed. Only the four expected files changed, and I found no secrets. The matching uses an explicit marker at the start of a line, which is the right approach rather than a word-guessing heuristic. One minor finding: queued requests that relied on "after <id>" for ordering lose it without a warning.
